Question: The distortion in space and time created by the mass of the Earth is extremely small, less than one part in a billion. Isn't that too little to make things accelerate at 9.8m/s2 towards the ground?
Answer: It is true that the change in observed spacetime geometry, time dilation in particular, here on the surface of the Earth is tiny. It is characterized by the dimensionless quantity G M / c 2 r ≃ 7 × 10 − 10 so indeed, less than one part in a billion. However, gravitational acceleration is a tad larger: it is c 2 / r times this quantity, which indeed comes to about 9.8 meters per seconds squared. So no, that tiny quantity is not too little, nor is it too great. It is precisely what it takes to accelerate things here on the surface of the Earth at one standard gravity. But one standard gravity is a tiny, tiny, acceleration when you consider more extreme cosmic objects. On the surface of something like a neutron star, gravitational acceleration is tens of billions of times greater. That puts neutron stars deeply in the relativistic regime insofar as gravitation is concerned. In contrast, here on the Earth, the consequences of relativity theory amount to, you guessed it, typically one part in a billion or thereabouts. Question: Apparently as a mass approaches C, further acceleration requires exponentially greater energy. But, if any non-accelerating object can consider itself to be at rest, then why shouldn't any subsequent change to its velocity be as easy as at V=0?
Answer: Oh, but it is just as easy. However, you must not forget how velocities are added in special relativity. So you have an object, happily traveling at… well, 0 m/s in its own reference frame. It’s a spacecraft. It turns on its rocket engine briefly and accelerates to 1 m/s relative to its earlier inertial reference frame. But this spacecraft was already traveling, say, at 299,792,450 m/s in your reference frame. Just 8 m/s short of the vacuum speed of light. And it turns on its rocket engine. So now you calculate its velocity in your own reference frame. Using, say, v 0 and Δ v for the initial velocity and the change in velocity, you use the relativistic velocity addition formula compute v = ( v 0 + Δ v ) / ( 1 + v 0 Δ v / c 2 ) and get… 299,792,450.00000005337 m/s. In other words, in your reference frame, the object’s velocity increased by just over 53 nanometers per second. For a more elaborate exposition of this problem, I recommend looking at one of the oldest Physics FAQ’s on the Interwebs, this description of The Relativistic Rocket. Question: Everywhere we are surrounded by a lot of visible electromagnetic waves. Why don’t we see a lots of black patterns of destructive interactions of light waves?
Answer: Actually, you see them all the time. Take a light source, preferably something that has a narrow beam of light. Aim it at a wall. You see a spot of light. Everywhere else on the wall, you see no light. (None from that source anyway.) Now take the wave equations that govern that light as it is emitted by the source and travels through space to arrive at the wall. That wave equation does not vanish outside the light beam. It’s there, everywhere. However, there is no significant constructive interference outside the projected spot of light. Destructive interference prevails. The wall remains dark. How do I know? Say, I wish to solve the wave equations in this case to arrive at a robust, wave-theoretical solution of the projection. Again, the waves are there, everywhere, characterized by a messy integral expression in the mathematical model. That integral usually does not have a neat, clean solution. Rather, I am forced to utilize sensible approximations, for instance the so-called method of stationary phase. The method of stationary phase explicitly picks the light path that corresponds to the strong constructive interference between waves, and discards those paths that are characterized by destructive interference. The result is the calculated spot on the wall. I.e., the method yields the light path that I would calculate using geometric optics, as it tells me precisely where the spot of light will appear. Going beyond either geometric optics or the method of stationary phase, more sophisticated numerical methods might reveal something more than a single spot; the spot may be surrounded by concentric rings of light or similar artifacts, rapidly diminishing in brightness. Here, I have an actual example from work I’ve done in the past. Although this one depicts a case of gravitational lensing, the principles are the same: The image on the left shows an “Einstein cross” (four spots of light) due to a particular (slightly off-axis) gravitational lens, calculated using the method of stationary phase, i.e., geometric optics basically. The image on the right shows the exact same thing, but a more sophisticated numerical integration reveals that there is also light between the spots. In any case, the key message should be clear. The very fact that, despite the fundamental wave nature of light, we see the result of geometric optics everywhere — rays of light, spots of light, shadows, etc., indeed the very fact that our eyes work and can form sharp images — is a result of the combined effects of constructive and destructive interference. In these two images, too, light is everywhere; it’s just that in places where the image appears black, destructive interference won the game. Question: Do white holes emit Hawking radiation? If no, then would it be the absolute opposite? If so, how would it affect the white hole and space time around it?
Answer: White holes are theoretical constructs, time-reversed versions of the Schwarzschild (or Kerr) solutions of general relativity. Take the words, “time-reversed”, very seriously. The Schwarzschild solution is not about the object that is the source of gravitation. It is about the gravitational field everywhere surrounding that object, all the way to infinity. In other words, the entire cosmos. So when we say “time reversed”, we are talking about a time-reversed cosmos. Hawking radiation is predicted based on an analysis that places quantum field theory in the curved spacetime background of a gravitating object. Contrary to popularizations, the radiation arises not because of the presence of an event horizon (which, in the case of black holes, remains forever in any outside observer’s future) but because of a past-future asymmetry in an object in a state of perpetual collapse. Now reverse time and see what you get! Incoming radiation. That’s what a white hole does. It absorbs Hawking radiation due to its gravitational vacuum polarization. How can that be? Again, take time-reversed very seriously. Think about this for a moment. You can’t fall into a white hole, right? But wait… a white hole still has attractive gravity! Time-reversed means that something orbiting a white hole would be going backwards compared to what you might see under identical circumstances near a black hole, but when you go backwards around a circle, it’s still a circle. So why can you not fall into a white hole? Because you are not in the white hole in the future. Again, time-reversed. It means causality is thrown out the window, and the future determines the past or the present. Compared to that, the idea that the white hole’s gravitational vacuum polarization somehow causes the rest of the universe to contribute to its “negative” Hawking radiation almost sounds quaint.
